name: Maibock
title: Maibock: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Maibock, or Helles Bock, explained: a strong pale German lager for spring. How it tastes, how it differs from bock, Indian pairings and examples.
tagline: The pale, hoppier bock. Strong enough to warm you, bright enough for spring.
tastes:
Maibock is the pale member of the bock family, brewed for the spring tapping season in Bavaria, hence the name May bock. You will also see it called helles bock. Take a bock, swap most of the Munich malt for Pilsner malt, raise the hops a little, and you are close.

The result tastes of fresh bread and honey rather than toast and caramel, with a clean, firm bitterness and a little spicy or floral hop aroma from German varieties. It carries 6 to 7 percent alcohol or more, but it is drier and more drinkable than its darker cousins, and the alcohol hides well. Like any bock, it needs long, cold lagering, which strips away the sulphur and rough edges of young lager and leaves a beer that is bright, smooth and clean. If it tastes buttery or fruity, something went wrong in the fermenter.

profile.look: Deep gold to light amber, brilliantly clear, with a persistent, creamy white head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Bready, lightly honeyed pale malt with a touch of toast. Spicy or floral German hops in the aroma and a clean lager finish.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium body, moderate to high carbonation, smooth, with a dry finish and some warmth.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner malt with some Munich or Vienna, German noble hops such as Hallertau or Tettnang, and a clean lager yeast.

in_india: Maibock is the bock most Indian drinkers will enjoy on first try. It is pale and familiar, close to the strong lagers people already know, but with more malt flavour and a cleaner finish. Bengaluru has seen fruit versions, with mango a natural fit for April and May. Because it is a lager that needs weeks in a cold tank, expect it as a seasonal tap, not in bottles. Serve it cold but not frozen, or the malt disappears.

pairings.why: Bright malt and firm bitterness stand up to the red chilli and cut through the ghee.
The beer's carbonation lifts the fried bread, and its malt likes the tangy chickpeas.
A crisp, malty lager with fried fish and lemon is a simple, reliable match.
Mango sweetness meets honeyed malt, and the hop bitterness keeps it from cloying.
